Akoni Kaeo: Kaeo processes coverage at an exceptional speed and puts the ball where only his receiver can reach it. He anticipates openings before receivers make their breaks and controls the tempo from the pocket. His command and surgical placement give USC a rare quarterback prospect with franchise-defining upside.
Chris Nwachukwu: Nwachukwu makes quick reads from the pocket, delivers polished throws, and turns an open lane into an explosive gain. Ohio State can make a defense account for his arm and legs on the same play. His processing and burst give him the ceiling of an elite dual-threat starter.
Justin Williams: Williams separates with precise routes, adjusts to difficult throws, and changes direction naturally after the catch. Colorado can target him at different depths and give him room to create once the ball arrives. His combination of route craft, hands, and open-field creativity gives him elite upside as a featured receiver.
Xavion Hill: Hill mirrors releases with quick feet and stays balanced when receivers change direction. His recovery burst lets him close separation and get back in position to challenge the catch. Michigan has an elite man-coverage prospect who can match shifty receivers step for step and take on demanding assignments.
Amari Brown: Brown separates in tight spaces with an explosive change of direction and keeps his balance through contact. He secures difficult throws and can get back to full speed quickly after the catch. Alabama can use his elite quickness and hands to create explosive plays from short targets.
Kyan Stokes: Stokes arrived at Oklahoma after starting at Louisville as a former five-star recruit. His acceleration gives him a way to extend plays and punish a defense when a rush lane opens. Oklahoma can build movement into the passing game and let his running ability stress the edge.
DaMarco Murphy: Murphy jumps off the snap and bends around tackles without giving up speed. At 6-foot-4, he covers ground quickly and keeps working toward the quarterback when the pocket shifts. Texas has a dangerous edge rusher who can force opposing tackles to account for his first step.
Kofi Singleton: Singleton uses his 6-foot-3 frame and long reach to disrupt releases in press coverage. He turns smoothly enough to stay attached when receivers break into their routes and can use his length to contest the catch. Georgia has a physical boundary corner built for demanding man assignments.
Connor O'Malley: O’Malley wins the first exchange with powerful hands and can drive a tackle back into the pocket. His 275-pound frame gives him the strength to keep moving through contact and take away space from the quarterback. Ohio State can count on him to generate pressure with power from the edge.
Ashton Johnston: Johnston gets out of his stance smoothly and stays balanced as he matches speed around the corner. The 6-foot-7 Ohio State tackle moves fluidly for his size, giving him the range to protect the blind side against quick rushers. His footwork gives him long-term starter upside.
